subtype: Following a boss into a grey area [Actor]
passage: I am Sabina, and this is about the form I backdated. Wasim, my manager, came to my desk on a Friday. "Just put last Monday's date on the safety checklist. The inspection is Tuesday, and it was done anyway, more or less." Two colleagues were within earshot, and one looked up and then down at a screen. I said "Okay" before my brain caught up. I told myself it was his call and he was the one signing. I typed the old date, and my hands felt oddly cold. That night I realised nobody had forced me. I had simply been handed a way not to decide.

qa.q: Which date did Sabina type on the safety checklist?
qa.a: Sabina typed last Monday's date on the safety checklist.

qa.q: Why did Sabina say "Okay" before thinking it through?
qa.a: Sabina felt the decision belonged to Wasim, which brought a brief relief; the cold hands suggest an uneasy sense that this was not really acceptable.

qa.q: What could Sabina have done at the desk instead of saying "Okay"?
qa.a: Sabina could have asked "is this okay?", asked for the request in writing, or taken the question to the proper channel, since following a request does not remove personal responsibility.

qa.q: How might the colleague who looked up and then down have been feeling?
qa.a: That colleague may have felt uncomfortable but unwilling to step in, assuming, like Sabina, that it was not their decision to make.

grounding: An employee complies with a manager's request to backdate a form, telling themselves it is not their decision, with responsibility diffused.

subtype: Following a boss into a grey area [Actor]
passage: Compliance note, Thursday. Samir, a junior engineer, changed two readings in the site report after his manager Vidya said, "Smooth it, the client is nervous." In the corridor Samir told me, "It was not my decision," and looked relieved and sick at the same time. The two others on the team said they knew but had not thought it was theirs to raise. I told Samir that a request from a manager does not remove personal responsibility and that he can ask for it in writing. The same day I raised the report with the head of quality, who has asked for the original readings to be restored. — Naveen, compliance officer

qa.q: How many readings did Samir change in the site report?
qa.a: Samir changed two readings in the site report.

qa.q: What does Samir's look of being relieved and sick at once suggest about how Samir feels?
qa.a: It suggests guilt mixed with relief: saying "It was not my decision" moves the weight elsewhere, yet Samir knows the change was wrong.

qa.q: What steps did Naveen take that put Samir on a safer footing?
qa.a: Naveen told Samir personal responsibility remains and to ask for such requests in writing, and raised the report with the head of quality the same day so the readings could be restored.

qa.q: Why might the two others on the team have stayed silent although they knew?
qa.a: They may have felt it was not theirs to raise, each assuming someone else or the manager would handle it; the responsibility was spread thin between them.

grounding: An employee smooths a report at a manager's request, telling themselves it is not their decision, as diffused responsibility does.
